name: Counselor Chad
logline: Every night this week the drained quarry lake comes back to Crystal Street, a little deeper each time, and out of it wades a seven-foot camp counselor with a whistle, a clipboard and a canoe paddle, enforcing the rules on every teenager he catches not watching.
backstory: Before Glimmer Falls existed, the land under Crystal Street was the Crystal Springs quarry lake, and on its shore stood Camp Crystal Pines. In August 1957 twelve-year-old Chad Mercer was the most enthusiastic camper there: toy whistle, borrowed clipboard, a habit of reminding everyone of the rules. He wanted to be a counselor more than anything. He also could not swim, because nobody had ever had time to teach him, and he was too embarrassed to say so, so he pencilled SWIMMER over BEGINNER on his own swim card. On the last night of camp the director, Harlan Pratt, saved on staff by leaving two sixteen-year-old junior counselors alone with forty kids at the night swim, no lifeguard, while he played poker in the lodge. The two teens looked away for one minute, at each other. Chad swam for the raft to impress them. Afterward Pratt told the newspaper his counselors had been "necking on the dock," and the whole county agreed it was the teenagers' fault. They even made a swim-safety poster out of it: ALWAYS SWIM WITH A BUDDY. DON'T BE A CHAD. Two years later the lake was drained and Crystal Street was built on the lakebed. Now the Heartstone has called the water back, and Chad with it: grown in death into the counselor he always wanted to be, waterlogged and enormous in red short-shorts and knee socks, his voice still cracking like a twelve-year-old's, blowing his whistle at every teen who is not watching someone else.

centralIssue.title: Neglect, and blaming the teens
centralIssue.summary: Chad was not a cautionary tale, and the two teenagers on the dock were not the reason he drowned. A grown-up left kids in charge of kids, then blamed the kids, and the town turned a lonely boy into a punchline. Chad rages at every teen who looks away, but what he never had was someone who would get in the water with him. Find his swim card, hear the counselor's side, and learn what his mother wrote, then teach him he is not alone in the water.

poster: A towering waterlogged camp counselor in red short-shorts, knee socks and a faded camp staff t-shirt rising out of black lake water that floods a suburban cul-de-sac at night, a silver whistle in his teeth, a clipboard in one hand and a canoe paddle in the other, an old swimming raft floating over a glowing purple geode beneath the water, teens on porch roofs shining flashlights
portrait: Close portrait of a hulking undead camp counselor with a round boyish face, gray-green waterlogged skin, a crooked buzz cut dripping lake water, a silver whistle on a lanyard, freckles, wide hurt eyes much younger than his body, lit teal from below by underwater light
taunts: Buddy check! Where's your buddy? Nobody? Figures.
Rule number one: it's always the teenagers' fault.
I passed my swim test. I passed it. I PASSED IT.

clues.title: Chad's swim card
clues.hint: When Camp Crystal Pines was torn down, its office trailer and campers' footlockers were hauled to Rusty's Junkyard.

encounter.title: Lost and Found, 1957
encounter.place: A rusted camp office trailer, Rusty's Junkyard
encounter.text: Deep in the car maze, half swallowed by blackberry bushes, sits a mint-green trailer with CAMP CRYSTAL PINES OFFICE still stenciled on the door. Inside: bunk lists, a rack of rotted life jackets and a stack of camper footlockers. One has a name in careful block letters: C. MERCER, FUTURE COUNSELOR. A puddle of lake water spreads slowly out from under it, though it has not rained in weeks.
encounter.art: A rusted mint-green camp office trailer overgrown with blackberry brambles in a junkyard, the door stenciled with a camp name, inside rotted life jackets and a camper footlocker labeled future counselor with a puddle of water spreading beneath it

success.text: The latch gives with a gasp of damp air. A toy whistle. A clipboard with rules copied in a kid's handwriting. A letter never mailed: Dear Mom, I told them I can swim so I could do the night swim with the big kids. Nobody here has time to teach me but I'll figure it out. Don't tell Dad. And the swim card: BEGINNER, DOES NOT SWIM, with SWIMMER pencilled over it, pressed so hard it tore.
success.art: An open camper footlocker in a junkyard trailer holding a toy whistle, a child's handwritten clipboard, an unmailed letter and a swim card with a word pencilled over the official stamp

failure.text: The latch snaps back on your fingers and the footlocker floods from the inside, lake water pouring out across the trailer floor, cold and smelling of pine needles. Somewhere behind you, very close, a whistle blows one long blast. You get out of the trailer fast.
failure.art: Dark lake water gushing out of a closed footlocker across a trailer floor, a teen bolting out of the door, a whistle's shriek shown as a sharp line in the air

choices.label: Go through the camp's office files instead

success.text: The swim test log for August 1957 has one line crossed out and rewritten in a kid's pencil: Mercer, C., PASSED. Beside it, in an adult's red pen, written after: Should have checked. Under the log, a staffing memo from Director Pratt: Night swim, 40 campers, J. Kessler and B. Teague (age 16) supervising. Lifeguard not required. Save the expense.
success.art: A teenager reading a water-stained 1957 camp swim log by flashlight in a rusted trailer, a typed staffing memo beside it with one line underlined in red

failure.text: The files have turned to soggy pulp. Every page you peel apart shows the same printed poster, rotted and grinning: ALWAYS SWIM WITH A BUDDY. DON'T BE A CHAD. On the last one, someone has scratched out the cartoon boy's smile.
failure.art: Soggy old file folders in a junkyard trailer revealing rotted swim-safety posters with a cartoon boy whose smile has been scratched out

clues.title: What happened on the dock
clues.hint: The school nurse at Glimmer Falls High was a junior counselor at Camp Crystal Pines in 1957. She has never once gone near the pool.

encounter.title: The Nurse's Office
encounter.text: Nurse Judy Kessler keeps a bowl of butterscotch candies, a cot with a scratchy blanket and, on the wall where she can see it from her desk, an old swim-safety poster: a cartoon boy sinking under cartoon waves, ALWAYS SWIM WITH A BUDDY. DON'T BE A CHAD. Every other poster in the school was taken down years ago. She keeps this one up. Her hands, you notice, shake whenever the water fountain in the hall runs.
encounter.art: A small school nurse's office with a cot and a bowl of butterscotch candies, a middle-aged nurse at her desk staring at a faded swim-safety placard of a cartoon boy sinking under waves

choices.label: Ask her gently why she keeps that poster up

success.text: She is quiet a long time. "Because I was the counselor on the dock. I was sixteen. Bobby Teague and I had forty kids and no lifeguard, and I looked at him for one minute, because I'd never been kissed." She folds her hands. "Mr. Pratt was in the lodge playing poker. He told the paper we were necking. We were kids watching kids. I've spent twenty-nine years being the girl who drowned Chad Mercer."
success.art: A middle-aged school nurse speaking quietly at her desk with tears in her eyes, a teenager sitting on the edge of the cot listening, the old swim-team pennant on the wall between them

failure.text: Nurse Kessler's face closes like a door. "Do you have a fever? No? Then back to class." As you go, the water fountain in the hall turns on by itself and runs and runs, overflowing onto the linoleum, and behind you she starts, very quietly, to cry.
failure.art: A school hallway water fountain overflowing onto linoleum by itself, a teen walking away, a nurse's office door half closed behind them

choices.label: Fake a stomachache and lie on the cot to look around

success.text: While she gets you ginger ale, you see it: a framed photo in her desk drawer, two teenagers in camp staff shirts laughing on a dock, and a newspaper clipping, COUNSELORS' CARELESSNESS BLAMED IN CAMP DROWNING. Someone has written across it in red ink, decades ago: WHERE WAS THE LIFEGUARD, HARLAN? When she comes back, you tell her what you saw, and she tells you everything.
success.art: A teenager on a nurse's cot peeking into an open desk drawer at a framed photo of two teen camp counselors on a dock and an old newspaper clipping scrawled with red ink

failure.text: She takes your temperature, and the thermometer reads 57 degrees, the temperature of a quarry lake at night. You both stare at it. The scratchy blanket on the cot is suddenly soaking wet. Nurse Kessler sends you home and locks her door.
failure.art: A nurse holding up a glass thermometer reading impossibly low, a teen on a cot under a suddenly dripping wet blanket, both staring in alarm

clues.title: Nobody had time
clues.hint: Chad Mercer is buried at the far edge of Pinecrest Cemetery. The parish register at St. Jude's lists who came to his funeral.

encounter.title: The Small Grave
encounter.text: Chad's headstone is small and tilted, at the very edge of Pinecrest where the mowers do not reach. Beside it lies his mother's, newer, with words carved too small to read from the path. Someone has left an old cork life ring leaning against Chad's stone, sun-bleached and recent. The grass around the grave is soaking wet in a perfect circle, and it is a dry October afternoon.
encounter.art: A small tilted child's headstone at the overgrown edge of a cemetery beside a newer adult headstone, a sun-bleached cork life ring leaning against it, a perfect circle of wet grass around the grave on a dry autumn afternoon

choices.label: Ask Father Iggy to open the 1957 parish register

success.text: Iggy finds the page. Funeral of Chad Mercer, age 12. Attending: his mother. Two camp counselors, who stood at the back. The director sent flowers and did not attend. His father did not attend. In the margin, in an old priest's hand: The boy never learned to swim. His mother says nobody ever had time to teach him. Iggy closes the book softly. "So the poor kid was alone in the water. Then alone here, too."
success.art: A young priest in a clerical collar and band t-shirt showing a teenager a handwritten entry in an old parish register at a wooden church desk, afternoon light through stained glass

failure.text: The register is in a locked cabinet, and the key is missing. While you search, every holy water font in St. Jude's starts to overflow at once, quietly, a little lake spreading down the aisle. Iggy blesses the puddle out of habit, then hustles you outside.
failure.art: Holy water fonts overflowing in a quiet church, water spreading down the center aisle between the pews, a priest and a teen backing away

choices.label: Kneel and scrub the moss off his mother's headstone

success.text: The water soaks your knees, cold as a lake, but you keep scrubbing. The words come up out of the moss: RUTH MERCER, 1921 to 1970. And under that, the line she chose: HE NEVER LEARNED TO SWIM. NOBODY HAD TIME TO TEACH HIM. I WISH I HAD. As you read it, the wet circle around Chad's grave slowly soaks away into the earth.
success.art: A teenager kneeling in wet grass scrubbing moss off a headstone to reveal a heartbreaking inscription, the wet circle around a small grave beside it drying away

failure.text: The ground under your knees goes soft, then wet, then deep. For one horrible second you are up to your waist in cold black water in the middle of a cemetery. Then it is just mud, and you are just filthy, and a whistle is blowing somewhere among the mausoleums.
failure.art: A teen sunk to the waist in black water among cemetery headstones, reaching for the grass, mausoleums in the misty background

signature.title: Lights Out!
signature.text: At midnight the storm drains on Crystal Street start running backward. Lake water rises out of them, ankle-deep across the whole cul-de-sac, smelling of pine needles and cold stone. Then the whistle: one long blast. A shape seven feet tall wades out of the dark in red short-shorts and knee socks, clipboard raised. "LIGHTS OUT WAS AN HOUR AGO!" Chad's voice cracks on the last word. "Buddy check! Where's your buddy?"
signature.art: A suburban cul-de-sac at midnight flooded ankle-deep with black lake water rising from storm drains, a towering waterlogged camp counselor in red short-shorts and knee socks wading out of the darkness blowing a whistle and holding a clipboard

choices.label: Grab the nearest friend's hand and shout "Buddy check!"

success.text: You grab a hand and hold it up high. "BUDDY CHECK!" Chad stops dead. He looks at your joined hands for a long, strange moment, his whistle hanging from his lip. "Okay," he says, in a small voice. "Okay. That's the rule." He wades backward into the dark, and the water drains away after him.
success.art: Two teens standing in ankle-deep floodwater holding joined hands high, a giant waterlogged counselor stopping short in front of them, his whistle hanging from his lip

failure.text: You reach for a hand, and it is not there. Your friend is three houses away, running. Chad blows his whistle right in your face. "NO BUDDY? THEN YOU'RE ON CANOE DUTY!" You spend the rest of the night bailing your flooded basement with a saucepan, and his whistle never stops.
failure.art: A teen bailing a flooded basement with a saucepan at night, the silhouette of a giant counselor visible through a basement window blowing a whistle

choices.label: Splash for your front door as fast as you can

success.text: "NO RUNNING!" he roars, but you are already up your front steps, through the door and slamming it. The canoe paddle hits the door once, hard enough to rattle the family photos. Then nothing. In the morning there is a perfect wet paddle-print on the welcome mat, and a single, damp, folded camp rule sheet.
success.art: A front door with a wet canoe-paddle print on it in the morning, a damp folded camp rule sheet on the welcome mat, puddles drying on the steps

failure.text: You slip in the water and go down hard. When you look up, Chad is standing over you, dripping, and he looks almost sad. "This is why we don't run," he says, and writes your name on his clipboard. You can feel it, after that. Being on the list.
failure.art: A teen sprawled in ankle-deep floodwater looking up at a towering dripping counselor writing their name on a clipboard

signature.title: The Night Swim
signature.place: Crystal Street, now a lake, two a.m.
signature.text: The water is waist-deep now. Old dock posts stick up out of the roundabout, and in the middle of the cul-de-sac floats a wooden swimming raft, the Heartstone glowing purple beneath it like a sunken moon. On the end of somebody's driveway, which is a dock now, two teens from down the street are kissing, completely oblivious. And out in the black water, little Petey Marchetti, nine years old and in his pajamas, is paddling for the raft on a dare. Something long and pale is moving under him.
signature.art: A suburban cul-de-sac flooded waist-deep at night with old dock posts rising from the water, a wooden swim raft floating above a glowing purple geode under the surface, two teens kissing on a driveway turned dock, a small boy in pajamas paddling toward the raft with a pale shape moving beneath him

choices.label: Dive in and swim for Petey yourself

success.text: The water is shockingly cold. You reach Petey just as he goes under, haul him up by the pajama collar and tow him back to the porch steps, coughing and furious that he did not win the dare. Under the water, Chad surfaces just long enough to look at you, at Petey, at the two of you together, and sinks again without a word.
success.art: A teen towing a coughing small boy in pajamas through black floodwater to porch steps, a giant counselor's face just breaking the surface nearby, watching

failure.text: The cold punches the air out of you. Something grips your ankle, not hard, almost curiously, and pulls you under for three long seconds. When you burst back up, Petey is standing on the porch, soaked and fine, staring at you. "The big guy put me there," he says. "He said you weren't watching."
failure.art: A teen bursting up out of black water gasping, a soaked small boy safe on a porch staring at them, ripples spreading where something sank

choices.label: Yell at the kissing teens to look up and help

success.text: "HEY! KID IN THE WATER!" They break apart, see Petey and do not hesitate. One throws an inner tube, the other jumps in. Together the three of you get him out. Out on the water the pale shape stops circling. Chad's head rises, whistle in his teeth, and he watches the two teens wrap Petey in a beach towel, like he is seeing a movie he never got to see the end of.
success.art: Two teens on a driveway-dock pulling a small boy out of floodwater with an inner tube and wrapping him in a beach towel, a giant counselor's head watching from the dark water

failure.text: They do not hear you. They are sixteen and the moon is out. By the time you reach Petey he is safe on the raft, sitting next to Chad, who is showing him how to blow a whistle properly. They both turn and look at the kissing teens. Chad writes their names on his clipboard. Then yours.
failure.art: A small boy sitting on a swim raft beside a giant counselor who is showing him how to blow a whistle, both looking toward a kissing teen couple, the counselor writing on a clipboard

choices.label: Rip a life ring off the old dock post and throw it

success.text: The ring is rotten cork from 1957, but it flies true, landing right in front of Petey with a splash. He grabs it, and you haul him in hand over hand. As he climbs out, the cork ring dissolves into lake mist in your hands, and from somewhere out in the dark you hear a boy's voice, cracking: "Nice throw."
success.art: A teen hauling a rope attached to an old cork life ring, a small boy clinging to it in black floodwater, the ring beginning to dissolve into mist

failure.text: The rope is rotted through and the ring sails off into the dark alone. You have to wade in after Petey, and the water is deeper than it looks, deeper than the street could possibly be. You get him out. It takes everything you have.
failure.art: A rotted rope snapping as a life ring sails away into the dark, a teen wading neck-deep toward a small boy in black floodwater

signature.title: Inspection
signature.place: The shore of Crystal Street lake, four a.m.
signature.text: Chad has made camp. Every teenager on Crystal Street has been marched out of bed and lined up along the new waterline in pajamas, and he paces in front of you with his clipboard like a drill sergeant at a summer camp in a nightmare. "Camp rules," he reads. "Rule one: it's your fault. Rule two: nobody's coming. Rule three: everyone takes the swim test." He points his paddle at the raft, very far away. "Starting with you."
signature.art: Teens in pajamas lined up along the edge of black floodwater at night, a towering waterlogged camp counselor pacing in front of them reading from a clipboard, a distant swim raft glowing over a purple geode

choices.label: Point out the rule his clipboard is missing

success.text: "You forgot Rule Zero," you say. "The grown-up in charge is responsible for the kids. Not the kids." Chad stares at his clipboard. He flips the page. He flips it back. His lip trembles. "Mr. Pratt never said that one." He lets the line go back to bed, and stands alone at the water's edge, rereading his rules until sunrise.
success.art: A teen speaking firmly to a giant counselor who stares in confusion at his clipboard, pajama-clad teens slipping away behind them toward their houses at dawn

failure.text: "That's not a rule!" Chad bellows, and his voice cracks so hard it echoes off the houses. "If that was a rule, somebody would've..." He cannot finish. He blows his whistle until dawn, and nobody on Crystal Street sleeps.
failure.art: A giant counselor blowing a whistle furiously at the water's edge, teens covering their ears, lights on in every house

choices.label: Step out of line and refuse the swim test for everyone

success.text: "No," you say. "Nobody swims tonight. Nobody gets left in the water." The line goes silent. Then, one by one, every teen on Crystal Street steps out beside you. Chad looks at all of you standing together and his paddle sinks slowly to his side. "That's," he says. "That's what counselors are supposed to say."
success.art: A line of teens in pajamas stepping forward together in defiance at the edge of floodwater, a giant counselor lowering his canoe paddle in astonishment

failure.text: Your voice comes out a squeak. Chad blows his whistle. "Insubordination! Swim test, now!" You make it halfway to the raft before you wake on the shore, gasping, coughing up something that tastes like pine needles, with no idea who pulled you out.
failure.art: A teen gasping and coughing on the wet edge of a flooded street at dawn, lake weed in their hair, a whistle lying on the asphalt beside them

choices.label: Start singing the Camp Crystal Pines song from the poster

success.text: You only know the first verse, but you belt it, and Moose joins in with a baritone like a foghorn. "Crystal Pines, oh Crystal Pines, where friendship never ends!" Chad's mouth falls open. Then, very quietly, he sings the second verse. He knows every word. By the end he is sitting on the curb, his huge shoulders shaking.
success.art: Teens in pajamas singing a camp song arm in arm at the edge of floodwater, a giant counselor sitting on a curb with his shoulders shaking, the clipboard in his lap

failure.text: Your voice cracks on the high note exactly the way his does. Chad takes it as mockery. "Oh, you think that's FUNNY?" The whole line gets canoe duty, and you spend the night paddling a rotting canoe around the cul-de-sac while he shouts strokes.
failure.art: Teens in pajamas paddling a rotting wooden canoe in circles around a flooded cul-de-sac at night, a giant counselor on a dock post shouting through cupped hands

finale.title: The Last Night Swim
finale.place: Crystal Springs lake, which is Crystal Street, Halloween night
finale.text: On Halloween night the lake comes all the way back. Black water laps at the porch roofs of Crystal Street, jack-o'-lanterns bob in the current and the old raft rides over the drowned Heartstone, glowing purple from below. Every teen in Glimmer Falls is treading water around it in their Halloween costumes, too cold to scream. Chad stands on the raft, whistle in his teeth, paddle raised. "Nobody watched me," he says, and his voice is twelve years old. "So nobody gets out of the water. Not until somebody watches."
finale.art: A suburban cul-de-sac completely flooded at night with black water up to the porch roofs, jack-o'-lanterns floating, a wooden swim raft glowing purple from a sunken geode below, a giant waterlogged counselor standing on it with whistle and paddle, teens in Halloween costumes treading water around him

choices.label: Swim for the raft and wrestle the paddle away from him

success.text: You haul yourself onto the raft, grab the paddle and twist until it snaps. Without it, Chad staggers, slips and falls back into the lake with an enormous splash. The water goes with him, pouring down every storm drain on Crystal Street at once like a bathtub draining, and you are left standing on a wooden raft in the middle of a dry roundabout.
success.art: A teen snapping a canoe paddle on a raft as a giant counselor topples backward into the water, black floodwater swirling down storm drains, the street draining dry

failure.text: He is too big and too heavy and he has been underwater a very long time. He lifts you off the raft by your costume like a kitten and sets you back in the water. "Swim test," he says, and the lake closes over your head.
failure.art: A giant counselor holding a teen by the back of their costume over black water, about to set them down, the purple glow of a sunken geode below

choices.label: Blow the camp's all-out-of-the-water signal on his own whistle

success.text: You snatch the whistle off his lanyard and blow three short blasts, the signal printed on every Camp Crystal Pines rule sheet: swim is over, everybody out. It is the only rule Chad never got to hear. He freezes. Every teen kicks for the porches. And Chad, by habit, by rule, turns and wades out of the water too, into the dark between the houses, and is gone.
success.art: A teen on a raft blowing a silver whistle, costumed teens swimming for porches, a giant counselor turning obediently to wade away into darkness between houses

failure.text: The whistle is full of lake water and gurgles pathetically. Chad laughs, a horrible cracking laugh, and takes it back. "Nobody blows my whistle." He blows it himself: one long blast, which means everybody under.
failure.art: A teen blowing a waterlogged whistle that only gurgles, a giant counselor laughing and reaching to take it back, black water rising

choices.label: Form a buddy line, swim out to him and teach him to float

success.text: You hold up his swim card, Nurse Kessler's story and his mother's words, and then you do what nobody did in 1957: you get in the water with him. Your crew links hands, porch to raft, a human chain. Nurse Judy Kessler wades in at the end of it in her coat, into lake water for the first time in twenty-nine years. You take Chad's enormous cold hand. "It wasn't your fault," you say. "And it wasn't theirs. Lie back. We've got you. You're not alone in the water." Slowly, shaking, Chad lies back on the black lake, and a dozen hands hold him up.
success.art: A human chain of teens in Halloween costumes linking hands from a porch to a raft across black floodwater, a nurse in a coat wading in at the end, a giant waterlogged counselor lying back floating on the water held up by many hands, the sunken geode glowing purple below

failure.text: You reach for his hand and he flinches away. "Nobody gets in the water with me. Nobody ever has." He sinks out of reach, and the lake rises another foot. You have the truth, but he does not believe yet that anyone will stay.
failure.art: A giant counselor flinching away from a teen's outstretched hand and sinking into black water, the flood rising around a broken human chain

best.title: Buddy Check
best.text: Chad floats. For the first time in his life, or after it, he floats, and he starts to laugh, a twelve-year-old's laugh, high and astonished. As he laughs he gets smaller, until the hands are holding up a skinny freckled kid with a toy whistle. Judy Kessler takes the faded staff patch off her old camp jacket and pins it on his shirt. "Counselor Chad," she says. He salutes her, and the whole lake drains away like a long sigh, leaving dew on every lawn and a raft on the roundabout. That winter every DON'T BE A CHAD poster in the county comes down. Next summer the Glimmer Falls public pool opens the Chad Mercer Learn-to-Swim Program, free for every kid, with a sign at the gate that says GROWN-UPS: WATCH THE WATER. Judy teaches the first class.
best.art: A skinny freckled boy ghost with a toy whistle floating on his back on a black lake, laughing, held up by many hands of teens in Halloween costumes, a middle-aged nurse pinning a camp staff patch on his shirt, dawn breaking over a suburban cul-de-sac

good.title: Swim's Over
good.text: The lake drains down the storm drains at dawn and Crystal Street dries out by lunch, leaving nothing but a raft on the roundabout that nobody can explain. The town calls it a water main break. The swim-safety poster in Nurse Kessler's office stays on the wall. Every so often, at the high school pool, a lifeguard swears they heard a whistle from the deep end.
good.art: A dry suburban roundabout at sunrise with a waterlogged wooden swim raft sitting on the grass beside a purple geode, puzzled neighbors in bathrobes gathered around it

bittersweet.title: High Water Mark
bittersweet.text: Chad goes back under, and the water goes with him, but not all the way. Every basement on Crystal Street stays a little damp. Every Halloween after, the storm drains gurgle at midnight, and the water comes up an inch, then two, then stops. Nurse Kessler retires that spring without ever taking down the poster.
bittersweet.art: A flooded suburban basement with a faint waterline on the wall, a storm drain on the street outside gurgling under a jack-o'-lantern

bad.title: Swim Lessons
bad.text: The lake drains away at dawn and takes you with it. Every Halloween after, when the storm drains run backward and the water rises over Crystal Street, your crew sees you under the surface: in a faded staff t-shirt and a whistle, standing next to a big kid with a clipboard, lining up teenagers who are not watching each other. You look like you are blowing your whistle. Nobody can hear it.
bad.art: Black floodwater over a suburban street at night with the faint underwater figures of a teen in a camp staff t-shirt and whistle standing beside a giant counselor, worried friends peering down from a porch roof
